#846. More than F1 - Monza's captivating football story

Monza were formed in 1912 but did not play in Serie A for the first time until 2022

Think Monza, and the mind conjures up famous winning drives by Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher, and by Kimi Antonelli this year on the way to his first Formula 1 title.

Sporting theatre on four wheels is not all that this northern Italian city has to offer, though.

Just under four miles from the historic home of motor racing's Italian Grand Prix sits the 17,000-capacity Stadio Brianteo, home to Serie A football club AC Monza.

It's not easy for the club to capture attention, given European giants AC Milan and Inter Milan play at the San Siro, a 20-minute drive away, while the romantic lure of Como is less than an hour from here by train.

But Monza have their own captivating story to tell.

Founded in 1912, the Biancorossi - white and reds - did not even play in Serie B for the first time until 1951. As recently as 2017, they were playing part-time in Serie D.

Under the guidance of former player Giovanni Stroppa, Monza were promoted to Serie A for the first time in 2022. Stroppa was sacked after a slow start in the top flight, but Monza survived for three years before being relegated.

They then bounced back immediately, earning their place among the elite again in May of this year.

Now owned by American venture capitalists Beckett Layne Ventures (BLV), and with former Southampton boss Ivan Juric in the manager's chair, Monza have a clear vision for how they can make an impact in their crowded geographical market.

AC Monza have played at the 17,000-capacity Stadio Brianteo since 1988

I am speaking to Monza chief executive Mauro Baldissoni in an office at the Stadio Brianteo, having been given a brief tour of the club's training facilities at Monzello, less than a five-minute drive away.

The atmosphere is positive after a 4-0 win over Cagliari the previous night - the club's biggest ever Serie A victory.

Monza sit third bottom at the time of writing, a point from safety, but the club feel so much is in their favour.

"First off, Monza is on the outskirts of Milan, so the location is attractive for the players," says Baldissoni. "It's a good point of visibility for what we do.

"There is a point of attraction and point of awareness about Monza, because it is already known in the world for luxury sports through the association with Formula 1.

"The infrastructure at the club is larger and probably more efficient than Milanello, the sporting centre of Milan, because they cannot have all the teams from the youngest in the academy to the first team like we can. This province specifically is one of the richest in terms of GDP in Europe.

"So, you have all the premises to create a good project. And there is always people coming to watch.

"Yesterday there were people from Newcastle, Fulham, Southampton, Sunderland, Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund at the game, and there were others. If you come here, you can watch AC Milan, Como, [an] Atalanta game, Inter game, and Monza.

"Scouts and sporting directors can come for two days and watch different games at a high level."

England youth international Jay Robinson (left) celebrates with striker Gustavo Varela during Monza's 4-0 win against Cagliari in October

Monza president Lauren Crampsie was previously the chief marketing officer at Chelsea.

She is now of the founders of BLV, which paid â¬45m to the family of the late Silvio Berlusconi to buy up Monza.

Crampsie, 46, watched the pre-match build-up from the pitch before the Cagliari win, making sure all the details were in order. Afterwards, she is mindful to let the players and coaching staff enjoy their victory.

Young striker Gustavo Varela is the star of the night, scoring two of his 11 goals in all competitions so far this season, earning himself a first senior call-up to the Portugal squad.

Monza paid Benfica Â£2.5m for the 21-year-old, who is currently top scorer in Serie A, with nine in nine games.

Already there are big-name suitors sniffing around, doubtless willing to pay a fee significantly higher than the one Monza forked out.

It is a perfect illustration of the business model the club are trying to create.

"We always think the club's mission is to win games, but it is also about forming players that are part of their academy first and also trying to identify talents that can fit with the purposes and the style of the club," says Baldissoni, who spent 10 years with Roma before leaving in 2020.

"In Rome we were able to identify young talents like Marquinhos, who was 18 years old and able to play as a starter before we sold him to Paris St-Germain.

"There were others like Erik Lamela and Mo Salah. But in Rome it is more difficult because expectations are higher.

"In Monza the idea is the same. The pressure is bigger because the impact of relegation on revenues is worse. But the environment and the sporting expectations are more manageable for a young player who has more time to form his emotional background."

Monza fought off competition from League One club Leicester to sign Southampton's England youth international Jay Robinson on loan this season, with Juric's presence being key.

The 19-year-old has already played 10 times in all competitions, scoring twice.

The main entrance of Monza's training ground

Fiorentina, Roma, Como and Juventus provide a stiff run of fixtures for Monza heading towards Christmas, before an equally important match against Venezia, who are currently one place and one point worse off in the table.

Baldissoni is optimistic. His wider view of the football landscape is not altered by the knowledge that promoted Premier League trio Coventry, Hull and Ipswich all spent in excess of Â£120m in the summer, a figure Monza can only dream of.

Plans are under way to refurbish Stadio Brianteo, which has covering over a single stand.

"Infrastructure is the weakest point in Italy under the competition point of view, to compete with other global markets," Baldissoni says.

"But there are costs and there are investments."

He says the stadium is "an investment meant to generate more revenues".

"Of course, the Premier League's revenues are much higher than all the other leagues, so those clubs have a competitive advantage.

"But they also overpay players because it's Premier League. Maybe they get a player that I would like to have because they can pay more, but maybe I can find another player that is not that far away. Then you have to be able to form the player.

"So, you identify a talent early, and then you keep forming him to bring him to a level where some other players already are. Maybe then we sell him to Premier League?"

It's a delicate balancing act, but Monza are sure it can be done.

"Sassuolo made it to Serie A 13 years ago for the first time and until last season, spent all that time in Serie A. Atalanta was going up and down and now it's one of the prominent teams, targeting European competitions every year," Baldissoni says.

"This is out of the work they've been doing in terms of identifying talents, forming talents, and remaining competitive.

"That is the target. It is possible. Let's see if we can make it."

#845. Kate Middleton Reveals Theme of Her Annual Christmas Carol Concert

As Kate Middleton and Prince William prepare for the holidays, the theme for her annual “Together at Christmas” carol service at Westminster Abbey has been revealed.

Kate Middleton is already preparing for the most wonderful time of the year.

This December will mark the sixth time that the Princess of Wales has held her annual “Together at Christmas” service at Westminster Abbey, marking the holidays with an evening of carols and giving back.

Over 1,500 people attend the service every Christmas at the same location where Kate and Prince William tied the knot back in 2011. And the Abbey has continued to serve as an important landmark in the couple’s journey as a family, with their children Prince George, 13, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, 8, often joining their parents for the annual holiday celebration.

In addition to being an evening of carols, however, every year “Together at Christmas” also honors individuals around the United Kingdom who have gone above and beyond to help support those in their local communities and make them “feel supported, connected and less alone.”

This year’s event, according to an announcement from Kate and William’s The Royal Foundation, will “celebrate the power of love and kindness to bring people together, creating hope, connection and a shared sense of community during the Christmas season.”

“At the heart of this year’s services is the belief that small acts of care can have an extraordinary impact,” the announcement continued. “Whether through friendship, volunteering, neighbourliness or simply being there to listen, the services will recognise the many ways people help create environments where others feel safe, valued and able to reach out when they need support.”

In addition to the event at Westminster Abbey, there will be 15 carol services happening concurrently in local communities across the U.K., ensuring individuals who have gone above and beyond across all four nations are recognized for their efforts.

The announcement confirmed the “cherished” tradition will air in the U.K. on ITV1 and ITVX on Christmas Eve.”

The annual celebration marks a rare instance in which William and Kate step out as a family of five, with all three of their children. And not only does it provide a sweet look at their family bond as George, Charlotte and Louis grow older, but the event also allows for the couple’s children to show off their special talents.

In fact, last year’s broadcast saw a special duet from Charlotte and Kate, the mother-daughter duo sitting side by side at the piano to perform "Holm Sound" by Erland Cooper.

Alongside the piece of music, narration from Kate shared an emotional message about the spirit of the holidays.

"At its heart, Christmas speaks of love taking form in the simplest, most human ways," she said. "Not in sentimental or grand gestures, but gentle ones: a moment of listening, a word of comfort, a friendly conversation, a helping hand, presence. These simple acts of care might seem small, but they contribute to the beautiful tapestry of life to which we all belong."

For more updates from the royal family this year, read on.

Kate Middleton & Prince William's Son Prince George Starts School at Eton College

On Sept. 8, the Prince and Princess of Wales' oldest son started his first day of school at Eton College, a boarding school Prince William attended in his youth.

Prince Harry, Meghan Markle Return to U.K. for Extended Stay

Six years after stepping away from their senior royal duties and moving to California, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex returned to the U.K. for an extended stay.

While the move is not permanent, the couple—who touched down in England Aug. 26—reportedly enrolled their children Archie and Lilibet in a British school.

The king of Norway died after 35 yearts on the throne.

"It is with deep grief that we announce that His Majesty King Harald has passed away," the palace shared. "King Harald died peacefully at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet Friday 28 August at 6:35 AM.

His son, Crown Prince Haakon, asceneded following his father's death.

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV Dies at 34

After taking the throne in 1995 at just 3 years old following the death of his father, King Rukidi tragically died Aug. 27 at the age of 34.

“It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that I announce the passing of His Majesty the Omukama of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, at approximately 10:00 p.m. this evening,” Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki wrote in a statement. “This is an immeasurable loss for the Royal Family, the people of Tooro, and the nation of Uganda."

The British royal welcomed her third baby—a daughter named Adelaide Elizabeth Annina Brooksbank—with husband Jack Brooksbank in August.

“Named after three people we love and admire past and present, including her Great-Grandmother who we hold close in our hearts,” Eugenie, who is also mom to son August and Ernest, wrote in an Aug. 17 Instagram post. “Her name is part of English and Portuguese history, two places we love and call home."

Meghan Markle's Show With Love, Meghan Scores Daytime Emmy Nomination

Meghan earned her first-ever Daytime Emmy nod on July 14 for the 2026 award show after her series With Love, Meghan was nominated for Outstanding Lifestyle Program.

On July 7, British Justice Matthew Nicklin ruled against a group of high profile figures—including the Duke of Sussex, Elton John and Elizabeth Hurley—in a lawsuit accusing the Associated Newspapers, the publisher of the Daily Mail, of unlawful information gathering.

In the lawsuit, filed in 2022, the plaintiffs accused the newspaper organization of mobile phone hacking, landline bugging and even home bugging in 97 separate allegations.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, was arrested on Feb. 19, his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

The arrest came amid renewed controversy over Andrew's alleged ties to Jeffrey Epstein. (Andrew has denied any wrongdoing.)

Prince William and Kate Middleton Break Silence on the Epstein Files

The Duke and Duchess of Wales spoke out amid the release of millions of documents in connection with Jeffrey Epstein, sharing their support for the victims of the late convicted sex offender.

"I can confirm The Prince and Princess have been deeply concerned by the continuing revelations," a Kensington Palace spokesperson shared in a statement obtained by MS NOW Feb. 9. "Their thoughts remain focused on the victims."

Marius Borg Høiby, Son of Norway's Crown Princess, Arrested Ahead of Rape Trial

Marius Borg Høiby—the eldest son of Crown Princess Mette-Marit and step-son of Crown Prince Haakon—was arrested Feb. 1 for assault, threats with a knife and violation of a restraining order, Oslo police confirmed in a statement to The Associated Press.

The 29-year-old—who does not carry a royal title or official duties—is being kept in detention for up to four weeks over risks of reoffending after the Oslo district court granted the request. His attorney Petar Sekulic told the outlet that they are considering appealing the decision.

Høiby is expected in court Feb. 3 as part of a separate indictment regarding four alleged rapes between 2018 and 2024, as well as two alleged acts of violence against a partner and violating a restraining order.

His defense team addressed the allegations in a statement to the AP, saying that Høiby "denies all charges of sexual abuse, as well as the majority of the charges regarding violence."

Flora Vesterberg, Queen Elizabeth's Cousin, Announces Pregnancy

Flora Vesterberg, the granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II's first cousin Princess Alexandra, announced that she is pregnant with her and husband Timothy Vesterberg's first baby.

"Delighted to share that Timothy and I are expecting our first child," she wrote on Instagram Jan. 19. "We're truly over the moon."

Prince Harry Appears in Court for Lawsuit Against U.K. Tabloids

Harry appeared at London’s High Court Jan. 19 for the start of what is expected to be a weeks-long trial against Associated Newspapers—the media group that publishes the Daily Mail, The Mail on Sunday, and Mail Online—over allegations of unethical newsgathering tactics

Other stars including Elton John, Elizabeth Hurley, and Sadie Frost are also taking aim against the publishing company in the lawsuit.

Associated Newspapers has “vigorously denied” the claims, according to the BBC.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry Celebrate 10 Years Together

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex celebrated ten years together by sharing a romantic black and white video of themselves dancing in their backyard.

Set to Olivia Dean’s “So Easy (To Fall In Love),” the couple revealed that the clip was recorded by none other than their 4-year-old daughter Lilibet.  Alongside a camera emoji, Meghan—who also shares 6-year-old son Archie with Harry— added in the caption of the Jan. 16 Instagram post, “cred: our daughter.”

The couple also shared a throwback photo from their first year of dating. In the adorable snap, the pair embraced each other during a nature-filled getaway.

“When 2026 feels just like 2016….,” Meghan wrote in the caption. “You had to be there.”

The Greek royal family’s private office announced Jan. 15 that Queen Sofia of Spain’s sister died at the age of 83.

As the statement read, "It is with deep sadness that the Greek Royal Family announces that HRH Princess Irene, beloved sister and aunt, passed away on Thursday, January 15th 2026, at 11:40 local time, in Zarzuela Palace in Madrid surrounded by loved ones."

Her funeral was held Jan. 19 at the Metropolitan Cathedral in Athens following her death, with the burial at the Royal Cemetery of Tatoi.

Kate Middleton Celebrates Her Birthday With Moving Message

On her 44th birthday, the Princess of Wales shared a message on the power of nature to heal.

“Even in the coldest, darkest season, winter has a way of bringing us stillness, patience and quiet consideration,” Kate said in a voiceover alongside footage of snowy landscapes in her Jan. 9 video. “Where the stream slows just enough for us to see our own reflection, to discover the deepest parts of ourselves, alongside the whispers and the pulse of every living thing.”

She added, “I find myself reflecting on how deeply grateful I am. For the rivers within us flow with ease, fears washed away, cleanse and purify, come to peace with our tears and discover what it means to be alive, to be at one with nature—a quiet teacher and a soft voice that guides in memory helping us to heal in.”

Kate Middleton Makes Surprise Appearance With Prince William

The Princess of Wales marked her first public appearance of 2026 as she joined her husband during an engagement at the Charing Cross Hospital in London. The outing in support of healthcare workers came almost a year after she announced she was in remission following her cancer diagnosis.

#843. Homophobia on the rise in football - what is your club doing about it?

Rainbow laces were a common sight for several years across football and other sports

Warning: this article contains offensive language

Homophobia and transphobia are on the rise in English football, with new data revealing record numbers of discrimination reports in the game - so what is the Premier League doing about it?

Last season, with little fanfare, the league introduced a new LGBTQ+ celebratory activation in February, Premier League With Pride.

The lowkey launch contrasts with the landscape of a few years ago, when England internationals like Jordan Henderson and Conor Coady were proudly proclaiming their allyship.

"The one thing it [Premier League With Pride last season] was lacking was engagement from players," said Jon Holmes, founder and lead of news organisation and campaign group Sports Media LGBT+.

"Not only would you have the rainbow armbands, but clearer allyship from players - that was more around the late 2010s. That has been in decline."

A report last month from anti-discrimination charity Kick It Out says they received a new high of 1,744 discrimination reports during the 2025-26 season, a 25% increase on the previous campaign. In this, reports of homophobia rose 46% to 203.

Kick It Out said it had received 142 reports of discriminatory mass chanting during the season, a 41% increase on 2024-25 and the highest number recorded. These reports included increases in homophobic and transphobic chants.

A prime example is the 'rent boy' chant predominantly aimed at Chelsea players and fans, for which incidents had dropped since it was criminalised in 2022. However, the combined 24 reports of homophobic chanting in 2025-26 season were the most in three years.

According to Kick It Out,, external many of the incidents over the past few seasons can be linked to domestic and world events, such as the Supreme Court ruling on gender leading to the FA's ban on transgender women in the women's game, which it says led to a spike in transphobic abuse.

The first Premier League With Pride event included rainbow branding at grounds - but nothing involving players

BBC Sport asked all 20 Premier League clubs what diversity policies they have regarding the LGBTQ+ community, and how much of their budget is dedicated to such schemes.

Nine clubs responded to the BBC request. None said how much money they invest in these areas.

A Nottingham Forest spokesperson told BBC Sport: "The club commits significant funding to this important area, and has an Equality, Diversity and Inclusion lead whose role is dedicated to ensuring inclusion is at the heart of everything we do."

Some clubs do visibly engage with their local LGBTQ+ community. Leeds United have been a sponsor of the city's Pride celebrations since 2018. Luke Ayling, then Leeds captain, marched in the Pride parade in 2022.

Liverpool and Brighton are annually represented in their city's extensive Pride events, as are the Manchester clubs.

Manchester City host an annual Progress flag-raising ceremony, while Manchester United said staff marched in the city centre parade. They also ran a flag competition with LGBTQ+ supporters' club Rainbow Devils, with the winning design displayed at Old Trafford for all matchdays.

Tottenham said that at the start of 2024, Spurs in the Community helped launch a weekly football session for members of the LGBTQ+ community.

And for the first time this season, all 20 current Premier League clubs have dedicated fan groups for LGBTQ+ supporters.

"It feels like there is a renaissance in the LGBT fan movement," said Holmes. "There is a rise in homophobia, but it does seem like the authorities are sitting up and taking notice. We can feel a degree of optimism."

But it is difficult for Premier League teams to encourage LGBTQ+ allyship and diversity, when representation within clubs is a mixed bag at best.

According to Kick It Out, which gathered data on the senior management teams from 17 out of the 20 current Premier League clubs, just 0.3% of people in those roles openly identify as LGBTQ+ - well below the UK population average according to latest national census data, with 4% of the British population identifying as LGBTQ+.

At a senior coaching level, from 11 clubs which responded there is no-one from the LGBTQ+ community.

Kick It Out says, comparing the dataset to relevant census data, that if football's workforce was truly representative of local communities, over 100 more people from the LGBTQ+ community would have to be employed at Premier League clubs.

The Premier League previously had a high profile association with LGBTQ+ charity Stonewall's Rainbow Laces campaign - but this was ended before the 2025-26 season

Rainbow Laces started in 2014-15 as a collaboration between Stonewall, Paddy Power and the Premier League. For two game weeks, usually around the end of November, players would wear rainbow-coloured laces or armbands, and the colourful branding would be seen in grounds and on broadcast idents.

Holmes said by the end it was doing more harm than good.

"I think the novelty of Rainbow Laces wore off," he told BBC Sport. "It also became more newsworthy to talk about the controversies; it became more difficult for players to engage without difficult questions.

"Also, club media departments are more risk averse, given growing toxicity on social media.

"It has been misconstrued that players were forced to engage, I think it was because Rainbow Laces became de rigueur, and it was perceived that captains would need to lead with the armband and allyship."

Rainbow armbands were introduced in 2017 for captains, having first been worn by MLS club Orlando City following the mass shooting at Pulse, an LGBTQ+ nightclub, in the city in 2016.

But the Premier League held its final Rainbow Laces campaign from 29 November to 5 December, 2024, and it was surrounded by controversy.

Marc Guehi, then Crystal Palace captain, wrote 'I Love Jesus' on his armband in what was widely viewed as a protest against wearing the armband (which was not mandatory).

Ipswich captain Sam Morsy refused to wear the armband, while Manchester United scrapped plans for a Rainbow Laces-themed jacket during the pre-match ceremonies following an objection by Noussair Mazraoui.

Simon Blake, CEO of Stonewall, admitted to BBC Sport that by the end of its 12-year lifespan in the Premier League, Rainbow Laces in that form had run its course.

"When it started, getting a few people to wear the laces was success," he said. "When it ended, when a few people didn't wear them there was criticism.

"If a campaign no longer has a positive vibe, perhaps it is time to do something different.

"Everything must evolve and change, but visibility still matters, it is important not to throw the baby out with the bathwater."

Stonewall held its first ever Rainbow Laces Day on 8 October this year, to encourage LGBTQ+ people to engage with sport. It had no connection with the Premier League.

Marc Guehi and Crystal Palace did not face any action after he wrote on his rainbow armband

It is notable that the players most ardently against Rainbow Laces were also vocal in their religious beliefs.

Guehi has spoken of the importance in his life of his faith and was one of several devout Christian players in the Crystal Palace dressing room. Both Morsy and Mazraoui are practicing Muslims.

Both Holmes and Blake acknowledge that this may have had an impact on Rainbow Laces.

"The influence of religion is clearly quite significant, but I think more understanding is coming in too," said Holmes.

"We have seen many parts of life less willing to engage with Pride, and football reflects that. The nature of LGBT campaigns is peaks and troughs, and we are in a trough."

"We don't have any specific data about what people's beliefs and views are, but we are in a world where people have different views, even within religions themselves," added Blake.

"The important thing is about behaviours, and we must learn to live with people who have these different beliefs and respect them.

"I don't want to speculate, as it would be too easy to assume people of faith would not be inclusive, I know from my work across 30 years that is not true; I have worked with many religious people who are LGBTQ+ supportive. Freedom of belief is important."

The current picture is a difficult one for gay and trans people in football at all levels.

The grassroots game is where the bulk of the increase in abuse has occurred, says Kick It Out, which claims it received 140% more reports last year than in the 2024-25 season. Three quarters of these reports are from senior grassroots games, where the players are over 18.

Away from football, research by Stonewall published in October found 11% of LGBTQ+ people in the UK avoid the gym, exercise classes or sports groups for fear of discrimination. Among trans people, the figure rises to 29%.

It said 15% of LGBTQ+ people who had been to a live sporting event, or watched sport in a bar, in the past year had experienced discrimination there. This rose to 26% for trans people.

"What we know is that there is a lot of work going on around equality and diversity; we also know homophobia and transphobia continue to be rife," Blake said.

"We are in a world, whether at Premier League or grassroots football, where views that may have been perceived to be unacceptable are now being expressed freely. That influences peoples' relationship with sport."

Premier League With Pride will return in 2026-27.

"The matchday activations take place in February in line with LGBTQ+ History Month, when the league and clubs will showcase their commitment to LGBTQ+ inclusion," a Premier League spokesperson told BBC Sport.

"There will be two match rounds dedicated to Premier League With Pride. This means all 20 clubs have a home game during that period, providing an opportunity to highlight and celebrate the LGBTQ+ community in football and showcase the work undertaken to make the game more inclusive.

"There is no centralised activation lined up for November."

#841. Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss | Jonathan Wilson

Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival feels like yet another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago

Magnusson: And your time starts … now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet …

One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best available manager now, but who might have been the best available manager a few years ago.

The problem with football is that it never sits still. What was true once isn’t necessarily true now. What is true now won’t necessarily be true in a season or two’s time. Almost nothing is absolute. What works once might not work in a different context. The key to good recruitment is identifying to what extent somebody’s past success was contingent on their environment, and how they may behave in different circumstances. And that is very difficult, which is why only four managers have won the English league title with more than one club.

The possibility of José Mourinho becoming manager of United was first raised as Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. Mourinho has recently claimed he turned the job down; other versions of events have him raging in a Madrid hotel as he learned that David Moyes had been hired, seemingly because Sir Bobby Charlton, then a senior board member, was worried about his impact on the image of the club.

It’s impossible, of course, to say whether Mourinho would have been a success had he taken the job then. But he had the ego to ensure he would not have lived in Ferguson’s shadow and, although he had been bruised by the Real Madrid experience, English football still recognised his aura. He was still adept enough to win a third league title at Chelsea.

By the time Mourinho finally took the United job in 2016, though, events in his final few months at Stamford Bridge had undermined him. He seemed weary and fractious, the tactical doubts raised in his final year at Madrid had proliferated and there was a growing sense his methods did not quite work with elite modern players.

There was a lot of talk about him as a guaranteed winner, but there’s no such thing in football. Very few managers last more than a decade at the very top. Only the most driven personalities, the most fecund minds, can endure the process of constant evolution necessary to stay ahead of the pack for more than a few years.

It’s easy to see why a board would have looked at his list of honours and been impressed, but United were appointing a manager on the way down. Was that obvious at the time? Perhaps not, but there were warning signs, and it’s the job of those doing the job of recruitment to identify them.

With every appointment there are mitigations. Given the immense power Ferguson had, it would have been hard not to appoint Moyes when he had backed him. Yet if there was ever a time when he might have been the right man for United, it was surely six or seven years earlier; modern managers tend to peak in their mid-late 40s.

Louis van Gaal was 62 when he took the reins at United, enjoying a second coming after winning the Dutch title with AZ Alkmaar and an impressive 2014 World Cup campaign with the Netherlands. Perhaps the comparison isn’t fair in that he arrived as an elder statesman; nobody, other than perhaps Van Gaal, thought he would be a long-term appointment. But the idea he would bring calm after a period of turbulence was to ignore everything he had previously done. Van Gaal is many things but he is not a calming presence.

But again, the timing felt wrong. It could never have worked given he was preparing a side for the World Cup, but had he come in to replace Ferguson in 2013, as a hugely respected figure with a robust self-belief that was never going to care about breaking Fergusonian taboos, he might have been the man to see United through the awkward transition.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim were supposed to be the coming men, managers identified on the way up. Both seemed to make sense. Ten Hag’s Ajax had played astonishing football, had beaten Juventus and Real Madrid thrillingly in the Champions League, had come within Lucas Moura’s implausible hat-trick of a Champions League final. Amorim had ended Sporting’s 19-year title drought.

But it turned out they weren’t right. Ten Hag, skilfully as he managed Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit, seemed overawed by the job; Amorim’s insistence on playing 3-4-2-1 with a squad ill-equipped to play that way was one of the reasons Dan Ashworth expressed reservations, leading to his departure as sporting director.

It is possible, of course, maybe by this point even likely, that there is no right answer, that the mess United are in is insoluble, Old Trafford a meat grinder that will keep chewing up managerial reputations in perpetuity. But United’s board’s attempts to identify the rising star have been no more successful than their habit of appointing fading legends.

Which brings us to Mauricio Pochettino. He has done remarkable things: he may not yet have won trophies in England but he effected such an extraordinary transformation at Tottenham that it seemed not unreasonable they should be part of the Super League project. He found things difficult at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, but most people do. A last-16 exit at a home World Cup with the USA was about par. The question, now he is 54, is whether the sense of drift about his career is an unfortunate and temporary state, or evidence that he is not quite what he was.

Perhaps the United job will revitalise him and he will revitalise them. But this feels like another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago; that United, once again, are answering the previous question.

#839. What's at the top of Frick's Aberdeen to-do list?

Swiss club Luzern did not renew Mario Frick's contract this summer

Mario Frick arrives at Aberdeen with the Pittodrie side sitting second bottom of the table and a game against relegation rivals Kilmarnock first up.

Lose that match and they fall to the foot of the Scottish Premiership. No pressure.

Apart from the obvious, what is it that the new head coach has to do to restore Aberdeen to previous glory days and avoid becoming yet another managerial failure at Pittodrie?

Okay, maybe this was obvious. But it's Aberdeen's clearest weakness this season.

They have the joint worst attacking record in the league, having only scored 12 goals and routinely looked completely short of confidence in front of goal.

Kevin Nisbet, the club captain, has 14 goals for the season. Nine of those came in the run to the Premier Sports Cup semi-final. Behind him, no-one has more than two.

Most concerning of all is that the Dons' have created the lowest xG (15.3) in the league so far. Not only are they not creating very many quality chances, they're struggling to take them.

They have just 3.3 shots on target per match, with a shot conversion rate of just 7.3%. Both metrics are the worst in the league.

Only Falkirk have created fewer big chances (19 to Aberdeen's 22) - the difference being John McGlynn's side score them.

Getting the best out of Connor Ronan could be key for Mario Frick

One of the most frequent accusations that came predecessor Stephen Robinson's way was that his team lacked an identity and players looked unsure as to the tactical plan they had been told to carry out.

Given the Northern Irishman's clear style of play with St Mirren, that was a surprise.

His team in Paisley were known for their physically-domineering displays that were full of grit and graft. That wasn't the case in the North East.

Frick seemingly prefers a 4-4-2 formation, with the midfield playing in a diamond.

That might be bad news for new signings Tony Yogane and Lewis Smith, wingers who did get a look in under Robinson but struggled to make much of an impact.

Sticking to a consistent midfield will help with that. While Robinson regularly relied on Afeez Aremu in the middle of the park, the head coach often chopped and changed his midfield partner.

Of all of Aberdeen's 15 summer signings, Connor Ronan was the one that probably caused the most optimism. Another former St Mirren man, he impressed in his time in Paisley.

The Irishman won a move to Major League Soccer with Colorado Rapids off the back of that form and was also called up to the Republic of Ireland squad without winning a cap.

Eight goals from midfield in the 2021-22 season was a good return - and a couple of them were screamers.

Former Aberdeen midfielder Jamie McGrath recently reminded his old fanbase that they could do with replacing him after he scored a rocket for Hibs in the 4-0 win that did for Robinson.

Ronan could be the answer, playing in a similar role with the same attacking capabilities.

He has yet to hit the heights at Pittodrie, but if Frick can make him tick, the 28-year-old could fire Aberdeen back up the league table.

#838. AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership

Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can

When you walk up from Haydons Road railway station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium.

AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.”

Kitcher was speaking before kick‑off in Saturday’s League One game at home against a Blackpool side dealing with a suspected norovirus outbreak in their squad. A superb arrowed strike from Alistair Smith and some vital late saves from Nathan Bishop ended Wimbledon’s winless run of 10 matches in all competitions. The 1-0 victory moved Johnnie Jackson’s side four points clear of the relegation zone and put a positive spin on a week that started with the fallout from the withdrawal of £87m of proposed investment, leaving the club’s finances even tighter.

Wimbledon made a £2.6m loss in the 2024-25 season – a figure expected to increase by £500,000 when they publish their accounts next month – which, as Kitcher pointed out, is not as loss-making as a number of other clubs in League One. Those clubs voted in the summer to reduce spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, but now many want to go further to curb the spiralling losses at this level. “It’s an ugly way of running a sport,” said Terry Hunt, a supporter who has been attending matches with his son Billy since AFC Wimbledon were founded in 2002 after the move to Milton Keynes.

Wimbledon returned home to Plough Lane in 2020, but had to create a bond to complete the move and the club still owe £7.5m in debts. In November 2025, the DTB warned that competing in the EFL at their new stadium was “not currently sustainable” under their structure at the time.

The makeup of the club has since changed. Supporters voted last April in favour of reducing their voting rights from 75% to 50.01% – the same 50+1 model that gives fans the final say on decisions at German clubs – and Wimbledon sought a cash injection. An £87m investment proposal from Sloane Street Capital, a venture including the sole funder, Omar Mir, and the former Chelsea and England defender Ryan Bertrand, was already being voted on by fans when Mir suddenly walked away last Sunday, citing a change in his investment priorities.

Mir passed Wimbledon’s due diligence tests, but the tech businessman was not a unifying figure. A Josimar report has detailed his “various connections to some of the most influential and controversial figures in football, technology and global security”. The 44-year-old did not attend either of the information evenings at Plough Lane after the proposal was first made in October, instead sending a two-minute video message, which meant fans could not directly ask him about his intention to purchase 90% of the economic rights of a fan‑owned football club.

“We really wanted to have some kind of knight in shining armour,” said Niall Couper, a former member of the DTB and author of three books on Wimbledon. “In this case, I personally wasn’t sure how shiny that armour was.” Couper, who raised questions about Mir’s background before his withdrawal, chose not to attend the Blackpool game owing to anger from some supporters at the deal collapsing.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

But the SSC deal is not completely dead. Bertrand and his remaining SSC partners Stuart Fiertz, Oliver Ward and Hugh Rosen – who would have owned 1.25% each of Wimbledon’s economic rights in the original proposal – have renamed themselves Sloane Street Football and are talking to other potential investors.

In the meantime, the board will seek approval from fans about taking out a loan of up to £3m to “manage the club’s cash position”, but they believe they are able to manage it through to the end of this season and into the next. Which division Wimbledon end up in next season remains to be seen – Jackson’s side survived relegation by four points last April and the manager will probably have his hands tied in January.

“I think we’ll probably go down, but bouncing between League Two and League One is absolutely fine by me,” Billy Hunt said. “The main goal is security and making sure we have a football club.”

#837. Vinicius says transfer interest affected Real form

Vinicius Jr signed a new six-year contract with Real Madrid in August

Real Madrid forward Vinicius Jr says he felt "truly overwhelmed" by transfer speculation in the summer, which has contributed to his mixed form at the start of the season.

The Brazil international has scored just once and provided three assists in 12 appearances for Jose Mourinho's side this season.

He was linked with a move to Premier League champions Arsenal this summer as he entered the final year of his contract, before signing an extension at Real.

The 26-year-old also says he did not train as much as he should have following Brazil's last-16 exit at the World Cup.

"I don't think I prepared as well as I could have after the World Cup, because the impact of that tournament is so significant for all Brazilians," he said.

"Being knocked out so early was something we hadn't expected. So, I took advantage of my holidays to enjoy myself, rest, relax, and spend more time with my family. I ended up training less than in previous years.

"That may have affected my start to the season.

"On top of that, regarding my contract renewal, with so many clubs showing interest last summer, I felt truly overwhelmed, as with the situation at Real Madrid. But it's a very long season."

Vinicius received a red card for violent conduct in October when he pulled the hair of Villarreal midfielder Nathan Saliba, which led to a four-match suspension.

In his absence, record signing Yan Diomande has made the most of his opportunity on the left wing, scoring four goals.

Vinicius joined Real from Brazilian side Flamengo in 2018 and has scored more than 20 club goals in each of his past five seasons.

Mourinho's side are second in La Liga, three points behind rivals Barcelona, and return to league action when they host Celta Vigo on Saturday.

#836. Phil Collins Walks With 2 Canes During Rare Public Appearance

Phil Collins made his first major public appearance in months at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame on Nov. 14, using the assistance of two canes during the evening.

The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame marked another day in paradise for Phil Collins fans.

After all, the beloved rocker made an ultra-rare public appearance for the Nov. 14 induction ceremony in Los Angeles, marking his first major event since May amid his ongoing health challenges.

For the occasion—which saw Collins inducted as a solo member, having previously been included as part of Genesis 2010—the 75-year-old walked the carpet in an elegant black suit which he paired with a white button-down shirt, the collar of which he left loose, and with the assistance of two wooden canes.

Collins was joined for the evening by three of his five children; Joely Collins, 54, whom he shares with ex-wife Andrea Bertorelli; Lily Collins, 37, whom he shares with ex-wife Jill Tavelman; and Nicholas Collins, 25, whom he shares with ex-wife Orianne Cevey. (The drummer is also dad to Simon Collins, 50, with Bertorelli and Matthew Collins, 22, with Cevey.)

In fact, during his speech on stage, Collins proved there will always be gratitude in his heart for his former wives, reserving a special shoutout for them.

"They loved me through the years, but more importantly, they have given me five great children," he said, per USA Today. "They are incredibly talented, and I made life tough for them growing up. But they have turned into such wonderful human beings. I love them to death."

The “Son of Man” artist—who in recent years has been navigating challenges with his kidneys, nerves and spine, in addition to type-2 diabetes—also took a moment to address his health after first taking to the stage.

“Thank you so much, I'm really not as bad as it looks," he told the audience, holding his canes aloft. "I'm much better."

And he thanked his longtime assistant Lindsay Evans for helping his health get back on track.

"Without her, I wouldn't be here. I'd be in a box, six feet under," he noted, saying Lindsay was able to show him his lifestyle choices were "bad, and she showed me what to do to make it better."

As for his musical legacy, Collins is still thanking his lucky stars for everything that has come his way.

"I've really been just very, very lucky," he said. " I grew up just wanting to play the drums. That's all I wanted to do. Everything else has been a very happy accident."

And when it comes to his future, and whether that includes a return to the stage, Collins teased there might be something in the air for fans.

“You haven't heard the last of me," he noted, "I can promise you that.”

For more stars who have spoken about their health challenges publicly, read on.

The Blink-182 drummer stopped smoking weed after being diagnosed with "precancer of the esophagus."

"I loved blunts and I would smoke too much," he shared on a November 2026 episode of the Big Bro with Kid Cudi podcast, recalling how his doctor said it was a "serious case. "He’s like, ‘This is your warning shot. Don’t f--l around. You’ve got to stop smoking."

The Jessie alum opened up about her "hellish" migraines, sharing how they've worsened after suffering five concussions over the course of her life.

"The brain injuries make things significantly worse," Ryan shared during a September 2026 episode of Mythical Kitchen’s Last Meals. "I had a pretty crazy, life-altering brain injury a few years ago, and I was out of commission for six months."

While Ryan described her first four concussions as "incidents," she said her fifth one was trauma caused by "sustained shaking over a minute of time."

Now, the former Disney Channel star needs to close her eyes to "think better."

"Quite often the world is really loud. It’s really too bright. There’s a lot going on," she explained. "The visual data that I'm taking in can be so distracting and so loud. Then, with the migraines—which are significantly worsened by that—it sort of is too much."

Brianna "Chickenfry" LaPaglia's Ovarian Cyst

In May 2026, the BFFs podcaster underwent emergency surgery after doctors discovered a large ovarian cyst that had been twisting her organs and causing internal bleeding.

"There was a half a liter of blood in my pelvic floor," Brianna shared in a TikTok video after the operation. "I have five incisions all over my stomach. They went in through my belly button with a camera so they could find all the blood."

The Total Bellas alum revealed that one of her breast implants shifted after an elbow slam from fellow WWE star Piper Niven during a July 2025 wrestling match.

"It's OK," she told sister Bella Garcia at the time. "We're going to get it fixed one day. I told the doctor, I go, 'Newly divorced, so the minute the boots are hung up, I'm going to come back to you and we're going to make these girls look real good, because these girls are going to get some action in the future and that can't look like that.'"

In October 2026, the former The Bachelorette star detailed how she cracked a vertebra in her spine after setting her vibration plate—a motorized platform that rapidly moves back and forth to promote muscle activation and circulation—to "level 30, supersonic speed."

"Seemingly, subtly, somewhere on the way to 30, maybe 10 or 20, my vertebrae turn crooked and rub against each other," Windey shared in a Substack essaye aptly titled "Broke back, no mountain."

"It was too fast vibrations I guess, and too many vibrations maybe, and too much pressure to shake," she continued. "And it broke. Broke right off, like your ex-boyfriend’s bumper. Well, technically, it cracked."

The injury left her with what she described as "insatiable" paresthesia—a medical term for a tingling, pins-and-needles sensation.

"This is the greatest sense of condemnation; of persecution, I’ll ever feel," she added. "And I do wish it on my worst enemy If only they hadn’t wished it on me first."

The 12 Years a Slave star was diagnosed with uterine fibroids—non-cancerous growths that develop in or around the uterus—in 2014, the same year she won an Oscar for performance in the movie.

However, it wasn't until 2025 when she disclosed her diagnosis, writing on Instagram that she had been "suffering in silence" for more than a decade.

"When we reach puberty, we're taught periods mean pain, and that pain is simply part of being a woman," she shared. "We're struggling alone with something that affects us most."

The Beverly Hills, 90210 alum revealed in April 2025 that he was recovering from surgery after his appendix nearly burst.

“Last week, I started feeling some pain in my stomach,” Brian said in an Instagram video at the time. “I ended up going to the emergency room, and I had a perforated appendix. Not quite burst, but just before.”

He added, “I'm on the road to recovery. It's not an easy process. This is my first major surgery.”

In July 2025, the Daisy Jones & The Six star shared that she had been hospitalized due to a hernia—a gap in the muscular wall that's commonly found in the abdomen or groin area—caused by wearing tight pants.

"'Suki you never tweet anymore,'" she wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter. "Have you ever considered I wore pants so tight 6 months ago it caused a hernia & I’ve been too scared to tell you?"

Savannah DeMelo's Mid-Game "Medical Emergency" Mid-Game

The Racing Louisville midfielder collapsed just a few minutes into her soccer team's September 2025 match against Seattle Reign at Lumen Field in Seatle.

The United States Women’s National Team player could be seen slowly sitting down on the field with a teammate by her side, per Reuters, as the referee called for trainers to check her out. She collapsed seconds later.

“Savannah received immediate on-field care from medical personnel and was transported to a local hospital for further evaluation,” the National Women’s Soccer League wrote on X later that night. “She is stable and alert."

Adam Devine's Long-Term Injury From Childhood Accident

Adam Devine shared that injuries he sustained after getting hit by a cement truck when he was 11 years old are still affecting him to this day.

“It’s been a nightmare,” Devine said in a 2025 episode of the In Depth With Graham Bensinger podcast. “I have spasms all over. For a while, [the doctors] told me I was dying—literally, within this last year.”

He noted that pain comes and goes, adding, "My body has all these things that are a little wonky and a little wrong with it."

The Bachelor Nation alum shared that he went to the hospital “crawling on all fours” due to overwhelming back pain that was aggravated during an RV trip with a friend.

“Right now, knees to my toes, it’s, like, still tingly, which is crazy,” he said on a March 2025 episode of his Trading Secrets podcast. “And to put in perspective, I don’t know, man, like not to sound douchey, but like two, three weeks ago, maybe a month ago, I was squatting probably like 295 pounds. And right now, I can’t do a squat on my foot. I can’t do a one legged squat, I fall. It’s like I had a stroke or something.”

But with the help of a back specialist and some steroids, he added, “We’re on the mend.”

Real Housewives of Orange County’s Gina Kirschenheiter shared her ex-husband Matt Kirschenheiter suffered a heart attack in March 2025, but thankfully survived the ordeal.

The 30 Rock star suffered a health scare at a New York Knicks basketball game in March 2025, leading to him being wheeled out of Madison Square Garden.

However, the comedian shared an update on social media the following day, noting it was a case of food poisoning and that he was on the mend.

The Even Stevens alum shared in February 2025 that she was shot in the face while on a trip to shoot clay pigeons to celebrate husband Brendan Rooney's birthday.

"There was another party with us and they unsafely fired in the wrong direction and shot me in the face," she wrote on Instagram. "@thebrendanrooney immediately sprung into action, assessed me, and rushed me to the hospital. I was hit in 5 places, one was less than an inch from hitting me directly in my right eye."

The Kim Possible alum continued, "Unfortunately a fragment got lodged behind my eye and it is too risky to remove surgically at this time. Doctors will continue to monitor me (I can see normally at the moment)."

The actress said she was grateful to be alive. "I love my daughters, husband, family, and friends so much," she said. "I saw my life flash before my eyes and I’m telling you, hug the people around you every chance you can. Life can change in an instant."

While the internet isn't always a kind place, Amy Schumer is happy that, in this case, it helped her get answers."The internet really came for me after doing a bunch of press, and I was like, 'OK everybody, relax,'" Amy recalled of her "puffier" face on a January 2025 episode of Call Her Daddy. "But then doctors were chiming in in the comments and they were like, 'No no, we think something’s really up. Your face looks so crazy that we think something’s up. And I’m like, ‘Wait, I’m getting trolled by doctors?’"After these doctors said they thought she had Cushing syndrome and that it may be caused by spiking coritsol levels or steroid injections, the Life & Beth creator thought, "Wait, I have been getting steroid injections in my scars.""I had a breast reduction, a C-section, whatever, and so I was getting these steroid injections," Amy said. "So it gave me this thing called Cushing syndrome, which I wouldn’t have known if the internet hadn’t come for me so hard."Toda, Amy is just relieved she's OK. As she shared in a February 2024 News Not Noise newsletter, "Finding out I have the kind of Cushing that will just work itself out and I'm healthy was the greatest news imaginable."

Casey Fitzgerald's Neck Injury From Hockey Skate Blade

The AHL player was cut by a fellow player's skate during a game in December 2024 and received 25 stitches. His father, New Jersey Devils general manager Tom Fitzgerald later told ESPN after his son was fully recovered, "We're very lucky. I don't wish that on any parent."

Hailey Bieber had the "scariest moment" of her life when she was having breakfast with husband Justin Bieber and started experiencing stroke-like symptoms in March 2022."Justin was like, 'Are you OK?'" the Rhode skincare mogul shared a month later on YouTube, "and I just didn't respond because I wasn't sure. And then he asked me again and when I went to respond, I couldn't speak. The right side of my face started drooping. I couldn't get a sentence out."While Hailey said the facial drooping stopped and her speech came back, she went to the hospital to make sure she was OK."They did some scans and they were able to see that I had suffered a small blood clot to my brain," the model added, "which they labeled and categorized as something called a TIA [Transient Ischemic Attack]."Later, Hailey went to the University of California, Los Angeles, where she found out she had a hole in her heart called a patent foramen ovale (PFO).She explained the blood clot had traveled into her heart, "escaped" through the hole and went to her brain, leading to the TIA.Hailey said she had a successful PFO closure procedure and was now feeling great.

The same year Hailey had her health scare, Justin experienced one of his own.In June 2022, the "Baby" singer shared he was diagnosed with Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a condition that caused temporary paralysis to parts of his face and forced him to cancel the remainder of his Justice World Tour."It is from this virus that attacks the nerve in my ear and my facial nerves and has caused my face to have paralysis," Justin explained in an Instagram video at the time. "As you can see, this eye is not blinking. I can't smile on this side of my face. This nostril will not move. So, there's full paralysis on this side of my face."In fact, he told his followers it had gotten "progressively harder to eat." But after a while, the paralysis went away."He's doing really well," Hailey said on a June 2022 episode of Good Morning America, later adding, "He's feeling a lot better. Obviously, it was just a very scary and random situation to happen, but he's going to be totally OK and I'm just grateful that he's fine."

While Jamie Foxx initially kept details of his April 2023 hospitalization private, he later opened up about what he went through.One day in Atlanta, "I was having such a bad headache, so I asked my boy, I said, ‘Listen, I need an aspirin,’” the Oscar winner said in his 2024 Netflix special What Had Happened Was... “Before I could get the Aspirin, I went out. I don’t remember 20 days.”Jamie said he was initially taken to a doctor who gave him a cortisone shot and then sent him home. However, his concerned sister Deidra Dixon then drove him to a hospital, where they got an answer: He had a brain bleed that led to a stroke.Twenty days after undergoing an operation, the Django Unchained woke up May 4 in a wheelchair and couldn’t walk. He then went to Chicago for rehabilitation and therapy."All I can tell you is that I appreciate every prayer,” he said, “because I needed every prayer.”

Tracey Yukich's Medical Emergency on The Biggest Loser

The reality star revealed that she "died" while running a mile during the first challenge of the NBC competition series.

“I don't remember a lot,” she explained on Fit for TV: The Reality of The Biggest Loser. “I remember hearing the helicopter. I just felt like I was floating. And then my grandpa was there. And then I saw darkness. But then I saw light. So I knew, I knew I died that day.”

“My organs were literally shutting down,” she continued. “I didn't realize that I had rhabdomyolysis. And rhabdomyolysis is your body's way of saying, ‘I'm going to shut down on you.’”

Emilia Clarke filmed battle scenes for Game of Thrones, but in 2019, she published an essay in The New Yorker titled "A Battle for My Life."Having a bad headache at the gym, "I reached the toilet, sank to my knees, and proceeded to be violently, voluminously ill," the actress wrote. "Meanwhile, the pain—shooting, stabbing, constricting pain—was getting worse. At some level, I knew what was happening: my brain was damaged."She was taken to the hospital for a brain scan."The diagnosis was quick and ominous: a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), a life-threatening type of stroke, caused by bleeding into the space surrounding the brain," the Emmy nominee added. "I’d had an aneurysm, an arterial rupture."Emilia had immediate surgery to seal the aneurysm, calling the pain "unbearable." While she was recovering, she continued, she experienced aphasia and was "muttering nonsense."A week later, "the aphasia passed," Emilia added, and she left the hospital a month after being admitted. At a 2013 brain scan, she learned a growth "doubled in size" and that she needed surgery again."When they woke me, I was screaming in pain," she wrote. "The procedure had failed. I had a massive bleed and the doctors made it plain that my chances of surviving were precarious if they didn’t operate again. This time they needed to access my brain in the old-fashioned way—through my skull."Thankfully, Emilia shared, she's now "at a hundred per cent."

Snoop Dogg's daughter Cori Broadus is grateful for her family.Because after she suffered a "severe stroke" in January 2024, her loved ones rushed to be by her side."I texted them that I just had a stroke and sent them a picture," she told E! News correspondent Will Marfuggi in December 2024. "Everybody just came to my rescue."Because of other medical concerns, Cori ended up staying in the hospital longer than she initially expected."I could have went home after my stroke, but my lupus wasn't doing so well," the Snoop's Fatherhood: Cori and Wayne's Story star continued. "My kidneys were failing. It was a lot going on."Today, Cori is on the mend."I'm doing great," she added. "I just had a little bit of motor skills that I had to work back on. But other than that, I was fine."

Shailene Woodley’s early 20s were not an easy time health-wise.“It got to the point where I was losing my hearing. I couldn’t walk for longer than five minutes at a time without having to lay down for hours, and hours and sleep. Everything I ate hurt my stomach,” the actress said on a September 2024 episode of the SHE MD Podcast. “It was this conflation of issues and diagnoses and different doctors telling me different things.”So Shailene—who chose to keep the exact condition private—set out to find answers. “I come from a very holistic background and study herbalism,” she added. “So I was very keen on, ‘I’m going to work with real MDs, [and] I’m also going to work with independent kind of healers.’ Just trying to search for some sense of comfort in my own skin.”It was a long journey—one that lasted for 10 years.“Throughout that decade, a lot of other things came from feeling so much discomfort physically,” the Big Little Lies star noted, “which was, ‘My gosh, if everything I eat hurts my stomach, I’m now suddenly afraid of food.’ And then going into the kind of mental f--ckery that can happen with that of body dysmorphia and confusion about identity and feeling safe in my own capsule, in my own skin, what that meant, and what that should be.”After tending to both her physical and mental health, Shailene is feeling much better.“It was a journey that ultimately physically resolved itself, and I am very healthy,” she shared. “I’m so happy to be able to say that."

#834. Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’

The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places

“Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona.

Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.”

The highs and lows of Sir Bobby Robson’s remarkable England tenure are chronicled in a new book co-written by Butcher: Almost Immortal – When Bobby Robson’s England Gripped The Nation 1982-1990.

Your name instantly brings to mind you playing on for England with a bandaged head and bloodied shirt. With hindsight, should you have left the pitch? Sian Williams

I never contemplated leaving the pitch at all. As the captain of your country, playing in a crucial World Cup qualifier against the top team in our league, in our group, there’s no way. I said to Bobby: “If you take me off, I’ll hit you.” I don’t think I would have but I said: “No, don’t do it!” Initially, I felt the blood and it seemed like a bad one, quite severe, but when I was bandaged up I could still play and it wasn’t a problem. Heading the ball wasn’t an issue because you’re really fired up, the adrenaline’s there, so it didn’t concern me. There was no way I was going to voluntarily come off unless Bobby was of a mind to do that, but he knew my pain threshold very well and knew I would battle on. I had numerous injuries before, broke my nose in 1982, five weeks in hospital and lost a lot of blood. So he knew I had great fortitude. Things have changed dramatically now. From a medical point of view it would have been right to take me off, absolutely. But that was then and I think, as a captain, you have to lead. It’s nice that people remember me through that image, but I was just doing my job.

I once stayed at the hotel that forms part of the FA’s headquarters at St George’s Park. Above the bed, and hanging over my wife and me all night long, was a giant version of the photo of you covered in blood. It was a bit disconcerting – but what’s the strangest place you stayed in or visited while on England duty? Stu Egan

I’ve actually stayed in that room as well. Stu has told us what it was like for him and I have to say it wasn’t great for me either. I’m staring up looking at me with a bloodied head and thinking: “Oh my God, this has followed me around.” At least when you close your eyes and sleep you don’t have to see it, but I’m sorry he had to stay there.

I didn’t stay in many really strange places with England. When I was manager of Motherwell we had a Scottish Cup quarter-final and were in administration at the time. I was organising our travel myself and booked a hotel near Stranraer, online. It looked great, right by a golf course. But when we got there we realised it was a residential home for the elderly. The rooms had accessibility handles and low sinks. It wasn’t a horrible place at all, quite the opposite, it was very warm and caring. But it was strange coming down for breakfast seeing people being looked after by the nurses. We won 4-0 so it can’t have been bad for us.

Now that time has passed and Diego has left us, has your perspective on that afternoon in Mexico City softened at all, or do you feel a professional duty to history to never let the “Hand of God” be forgotten? Victor Segovia

My feelings haven’t changed and they won’t. But I’ve learned to live with it better, I’ve learned to get through it and I’m not so annoyed by the memory. You’re just disappointed it happened. It had an influence on the game because we went one down and I think a lot of the players were shocked by what happened. Half the team saw it, half didn’t. I was one of the ones who didn’t. It had a big part to play in the fact we didn’t get switched on again and conceded the second goal. I’m more disappointed because he beat me twice. You’ve got to respect the man and respect what he did for the second goal, and what he did in that game. He was the best player I’ve played against and one that I never really got near.

Maradona’s “wondergoal” – it was really an own goal by you as you did a desperate sliding tackle, wasn’t it? David

If I’d got a touch I’d have raised my hand straight away and admitted it was the best own goal I’d ever scored. He went past Peter Shilton and I managed to get back, but I couldn’t see the ball so I was kind of feeling around him with my left foot. I couldn’t get my right foot across, but I thought I could block it. I was so surprised when he made good contact and put it in the net because I thought: “I’ve got this.” You can see me afterwards on the TV, I’m banging my shinpads, I was so angry. I was more angry about that goal than I was the “Hand of God” goal. So I’d have loved to claim that one. I know it sounds bizarre but it would have been one of my greatest achievements. Would it still have been the greatest goal scored at a World Cup?

In the early 80s you had a brilliant side at Portman Road so I wondered if you have: “If only …” or “What if …” moments about that time. It has always felt to me that Ipswich left another big trophy or two out there. Stooze

We did. The 1980-81 season was arguably the best in our history. We lost the FA Cup semi-final, lost the league title on the last day of the season and then had to play the Uefa Cup final, which thankfully we won. It’s always at the back of your mind that you missed out on what you should have got, which was the treble. We should have done it. But I think the 66-game season was just too much for us, we didn’t have a big squad and struggled with injuries towards the end. But we came really close. Look at the teams Sir Bobby built, we were in Europe for nine seasons out of 10. There’s no particular moment I sit down and dwell on, but you know it’s there, so close but so far.

What was the one quality Bobby Robson had above all others and was he the best manager you played under? Carl Parrish

His man-management was top class. He knew how to get the best from his players, knew what buttons to press and got to know them very quickly. He could wield his strength, he was a really tough guy, but when he was friendly it was lovely. His face lit up and he made you feel really good through that man-management. He always used to say to me: “Whenever I pick you, you always do well.” When someone says that you feel really good about yourself. He knew what to say. But had an abundance of things that worked really well for him. His tactical knowledge, selection of players, the network he built up for the younger players to come through – so many things. He was the most complete manager in my eyes and I still think he’s the best. Wherever he went, home or abroad, he proved himself in a way no English manager has done.

What was it like playing alongside Des Walker with England? And how close were England to winning the World Cup in 1990? Ahmed Kheyre

Des was the best centre-half I played alongside for England; he was unbelievable. He prolonged my international career because he was my pace. You never beat Des Walker. He was OK on the ball, it wasn’t his strength, but he used to give it to people that had great ability in that area so he was very astute. He was very young at the time, but dependable, talked well, shouted, pulled you about, was dominant. He was one of the reasons I made it to Italia 90. As for how close we were, I think the semi-final was the best we played all tournament. As I was walking out I felt so serene, comfortable, like I was in a dream state. It was never normally like that, but I could see our boys’ faces: steely, determined, but relaxed. It was the best I’d ever felt before a game. I even successfully backheeled the ball to a teammate. It was one of the best moments of our lives. We didn’t get to the very best one, the final, but we were so close. You’re talking inches, the shot that came off the post right between Lineker and Beardsley. Beating Argentina in the final would have been the ultimate redemption.

Is it true that during your time at Rangers, the top away scorer at Ibrox was Butcher (og)? Anonymous

I think I scored more goals past Chris Woods, my own goalkeeper, than any other Scottish striker. They were crackers: pick that one out Woodsy. He was my roommate as well, so he would say: “I don’t want any more going past me.” But they were all good ones, put it that way. They weren’t just ricochets or anything else like that. Wow, they were proper own goals. If you’re going to hit it, hit it hard.

I’m a massive fan of you as a player but think I’m even more impressed by your work with veterans following the death of your son. What would be the biggest thing we could do to support veterans? Jim

We’ve got to have a specific centre for veterans, like a St George’s Park, which would be dedicated to their health and that of their families. That would be the ultimate aim for me. We need more, and bigger, facilities to focus on veterans’ mental health and respite for those around them. It would be ideal to create a military community where you’re not in service, but the families are together. It would enable the veterans to relax, get treatment, get better, get the toolbox that provides the coping mechanisms so that if something happens they know what to do and where to go. My son didn’t have that unfortunately: he stayed in his room and that was his safe place.

I enjoy my work with Combat2Coffee, which supports veterans and their families. It’s doing really well and the togetherness is great. It’s getting exponentially bigger and we’re about to open a veterans’ hub in Ipswich. It’s a special thing, you can just walk in off the street and get that support. I’m doing this because my son would have loved it, and it’s what he needed.

#833. Michael J. Fox Steps Out With All 3 Daughters for Rare Family Outing

Michael J. Fox and Tracy Pollan’s daughters Aquinnah, Schuyler and Esmé joined their parents for the Michael J. Fox Foundation’s annual gala, marking a rare family outing.

Where Michael J. Fox is going, he just needs his family’s love.

The Back to the Future star was not only joined by his wife Tracy Pollan for the Michael J. Fox Foundation’s A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Cure Parkinson’s gala on Nov. 14, but also by three extra special guests.

When Fox and Pollan stepped out at the Waldorf Astoria in New York City for the fundraising event, they were accompanied by 31-year-old twins Aquinnah and Schuyler, as well as 25-year-old Esmé. The three girls each wore elegant gowns and big smiles as they posed on the event’s red carpet alongside their parents. (Fox and Pollan are also parents to 37-year-old son Sam, who was not in attendance.)

Pollan, for her part, donned a calf-length black shift dress and heels, while Fox wore a black blazer over a navy t-shirt and black slacks.

The gala featured performances from John Mayer and Brad Paisley, as well as comedy sets from Josh Johnson and Tom Papa, while actor Denis Leary helmed the night as emcee.

Fox started the Michael J. Fox Foundation in 2000, nine years after he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. In the time since, the organization has become an important player in the fight to cure the disease—with the annual gala acting as a way to thank the many hands who make executing the mission light work.

As Pollan told People at the event, “It celebrates everybody who’s worked with us for 20-plus years. Just the huge and amazing amount of money that’s been raised that goes directly into the scientists’ pockets, and they can just do all the work that’s necessary [to finding a cure]. We really are seeing so much progress.”

The 66-year-old also shared insight into how she and her family navigate Fox’s health challenges.

“I think you just have to do it day by day,” she reflected. “You have to look at what’s in front of you, and you have to stay in the moment.”

As for Fox, the Shrinking star has been candid about how grateful he is for his family walking beside him on his health journey.

In fact, when the 65-year-old accepted the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award at the 2026 Emmys, he specifically thanked his wife and kids “for their sacrifices, for their patience, and for their love.”

#832. Ratcliffe's Ineos Group settles £10m-plus claim with Ainslie's firm over yacht

Ineos Racing sued Athena Racing earlier this year, alleging the latter breached a deal between the two companies by refusing to return multimillion-pound yacht; Sir Ben Ainslie's GB1 team is the challenger of record for the next America's Cup in Naples, Italy in 2027

A company connected to Sir Jim Ratcliffe's Ineos Group said it has settled a High Court claim against a firm founded by Sir Ben Ainslie.

Ineos Racing sued Athena Racing earlier this year, alleging the latter breached a deal between the two companies by refusing to return the multimillion-pound yacht Ineos Britannia, which Ainslie captained at the 2024 America's Cup in a 7-2 defeat to Emirates Team New Zealand in Barcelona.

Lawyers for Ineos said in court documents filed earlier this year that the claim was valued at more than £10 million.

Athena Racing was defending the claim, arguing that Ineos was not entitled to have the yacht back.

In a statement on Monday, Ineos said: "Ineos has reached a settlement with Athena Racing and considers the matter now closed."

No further details, including whether the yacht has been returned, have been provided.

Four-time Olympic champion Ainslie hit out at Ineos Britannia in April 2025 after they confirmed their challenge for the 38th America's Cup in Naples in 2027 would not involve him.

Ainslie's GB1 team is the challenger of record for the event in Italy next year.

No British team has ever won the America's Cup since it was first contested in 1850.
