#816. Travis Kelce Exits Kansas City Chiefs Game With Ankle Injury

Travis Kelce suffered a tackle in the Kansas City Chiefs’ first quarter against the Atlanta Falcons that caused injury to his ankle, with the tight end limping off the field for evaluation.

The Kansas City Chiefs’ tight end exited the team’s Nov. 15 match up against the Atlanta Falcons after his very first catch of the game, suffering an apparent injury to an already tender ankle.

While Kelce received quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ 23-yard pass, the 37-year-old was tackled by the Falcons’ DeMarcco Hellams. Kelce was slow to get up from the hit but was able to limp to the sideline without assistance where his ankle was taped by the medical team. Rather than retake the field, however, Kelce made his way to the locker room for additional evaluation.

The Chiefs noted his return to the field as questionable.

Thankfully, since he was able to complete a pass before his exit from the game, Kelce has now achieved a milestone 200 consecutive games with at least one reception.

Not present for the injury or new achievement, however, was Kelce’s wife Taylor Swift. Though the Grammy winner has become a staple at the Chiefs’ home games at Arrowhead Stadium, Swift often skips Kelce’s away games, including the game at Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium.

But when she does take in the on-field action live in person, Swift is often accompanied by some pals in her VIP suite. Recently, she enjoyed an enchanting reunion with pal Karlie Kloss, who joined Swift at the Chiefs’ Nov. 8 home game against the New York Jets.

The pair—who were inseparable BFFs before a rumored growing apart in the 2010s—were all smiles and even shared a hug as they watched the game, with Kloss being joined by her and her husband Jared Kushner’s 5-year-old son Levi.

But even before they watched Swift’s guy on the Chiefs, Kloss and Swift had already proved they’d shaken off any rumored bad blood. After all, Kloss and Kushner were also on the 1,000-person guest list to witness Kelce and Swift’s nuptials in July.

And like any loyal BFF, Kloss refused to fill in any blanks spaces on what exactly went down inside Madison Square Garden.

For a look back at how Kelce and Swift went from missed bracelet connections to being the perfect teammates, read on.

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's love story began in July 2023, when the singer's Eras Tour made a stop at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Mo.

As a huge Swiftie, the Kansas City Chiefs tight end caught the show with hopes of giving Taylor a friendship bracelet with his number on it. However, he failed to complete the pass due to her pre-show rituals.

"I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs that she sings," Travis shared on the July 26 episode of his New Heights podcast. "So, I was a little butt-hurt I didn't get to hand her one of the bracelets I made for her."

After publicly recounting his fumble—a move Taylor would later describe as "metal as hell"—Travis decided to shoot his shot and invite the Grammy winner to watch the Chiefs play at Arrowhead Stadium.

"I threw it out there, I threw the ball in her court," he shared on The Pat McAfee Show. "I told her, you know, 'I've seen you rock the stage in Arrowhead, you might have to come see me rock the stage in Arrowhead and see which one's a little more lit.' So, we'll see what happens in the near future."

Travis was rocking a mustache—which he debuted in August during training camp—when he was first introduced to Taylor.

As he later noted of the era, "That 'stache and the 87 jersey was pretty iconic there for a little bit, and I had it when I met Taylor for the first time."

By early September, a source close to the situation told E! News that Travis and Taylor were "texting and talking here and there."

"It's been very low-key," the insider explained, "as he's been in season."

Accepting Travis' invite, Taylor joined the athlete's mom Donna Kelce at Arrowhead Stadium to watch him and the Chiefs take on the Chicago Bears. After the game, Taylor and Travis were seen packing PDA at a local bar.

Though folklore had it that it was the couple's first in-person meeting, the "Karma" singer later clarified the two had spent a "significant amount of time" getting to know each other beforehand.

As Taylor noted, "We would never be psychotic enough to hard launch a first date."

As an indication that the relationship was heating up, Taylor brought her squad—including friends Blake Lively, Ryan Reynolds, Sophie Turner, Hugh Jackman, Sabrina Carpenter and Antoni Porowski—to watch the Chiefs play against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

Another sign that Travis could be The 1? Taylor started bonding with Brittany Mahomes—the wife of Travis' BFF and teammate Patrick Mahomes—in and outside of NFL games.

The couple took their romance to TV, making a surprise appearance on the Oct. 14 episode of Saturday Night Live. Their Big Apple takeover also included the after-party for the NBC sketch show and a date night at the Waverly Inn.

During a bye week, Travis traveled down to Argentina to catch the South American leg of Taylor's Eras Tour. Not only did the NFL star bond with Taylor's dad, Scott Swift, at the Nov. 11 show in Buenos Aires, but he also got a special shoutout from the stage.

"Karma is that guy on the Chiefs," Taylor sang, "coming straight home to me."

After the show, the Midnights artist was seen running up to Travis backstage and greeting him with a passionate kiss.

Taylor addressed the lavender craze surrounding her appearances at Travis' games.

"I'm going to see him do what he loves, we're showing up for each other, other people are there and we don't care," she told Time. "The opposite of that is you have to go to an extreme amount of effort to make sure no one knows that you're seeing someone."

The music superstar turned Travis' Dec. 17 game into a family affair, bringing her dad to cheer on her man.

Taylor and Travis spent their first New Year's Eve together, sharing a romantic kiss when the clock struck midnight on Jan. 1.

Continuing to bond with Travis' family, Taylor hung out with his brother Jason Kelce and sister-in-law Kylie Kelce at the Chiefs' game against the Buffalo Bills.

Taylor joined Travis on the football field when the Chiefs won the AFC Championship, a victory that cemented the team's spot in the 2024 Super Bowl. The couple shared a celebratory kiss before exchanging the L-word.

"Tay, I'm gonna enjoy with the guys," he told her. "I love you—so much it's not funny."

The pair locked lips on the field after Travis led the Kansas City Chiefs to victory on Feb. 11, 2024 in Las Vegas.

Taylor posted footage of Travis on social media for the first time Feb. 12, poking fun at how she took her parents clubbing with the athlete after the Super Bowl.

Taylor's first Instagram pic featuring Travis was a selfie of the two with Prince William and his and wife Kate Middleton's eldest kids Prince George and Princess Charlotte backstage at the singer's Eras tour show at Wembley Stadium in London.

While attending his seventh Eras tour concert, and second show at London's Wembley Stadium, the NFL star joined his girlfriend onstage as a backup performer during her performance of "I Can Do It With a Broken Heart."

Taylor joined Travis for the Chief's first game of the regular 2024-25 season and appeared to re-enact a PDA moment from October 2023 in this photo shared by Chariah Gordon, who is pictured with her boyfriend, Chiefs wide receiver Mecole Hardman.

The two attended model Karen Elson's wedding to Electric Lady Studios owner Lee Foster in New York City.

The next day, the pair attended the men's singles final match at the U.S. Open.

The two stepped out for a double dinner date with Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds in NYC.

The pair stepped out for two back-to-back dates in New York City over the last weekend of 2024, matching outfits both times.

The pair spent the NFL off-season together, enjoying a snowy vacation to Montana with sportscaster Erin Andrews.

Travis posted his first pics with Taylor on Instagram in July 2025, including an adorable shot of them at dinner—which subtly revealed their phone lockscreen pics of one another.

August: 2025: Taking Their Romance to New Heights

Self-described New Heights superfan Taylor made her debut on Travis and Jason's podcast in a nearly two-hour-long special episode Aug. 13. In addition to very candidly detailing their life together—in and out of the spotlight—Taylor also revealed her 12th studio album The Life of a Showgirl, set to debut Oct. 3.

August 2025: She'd Marry Him With Paper Rings

More than two years after Travis' podcast shoutout heard 'round the world, Travis and Taylor announced they are engaged. Making a cheeky reference to her song "So High School." the two captioned the Aug. 26 Instagram post featuring their engagement photos, "Your English teacher and your gym teacher are getting married."

While Taylor would've married Travis with paper rings, the athlete popped the question with an old mine brilliant cut diamond sparkler he co-designed with Artifex Fine Jewelry's Kindred Lubeck.

October 2025: The Life of a Showgirl in Love

Taylor released The Life of a Showgirl, her 12th studio album that she recorded during the Eras Tour. Songs about her romance with Travis include "The Fate of Ophelia"—which included many Easter eggs about the NFL star—and "Wood," in which she cheekily sang that his "love was the key that opened my thighs.”

"New Heights of manhood," Taylor continued on the track, referencing the name of Travis' podcast. "I ain't gotta knock on wood."

Taylor and Travis made their first award show appearance as a couple at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards, where she won seven trophies including Pop Album of the Year for The Life of a Showgirl.

"The Life of a Showgirl was really inspired by the energy that I felt like looking into crowds and seeing you guys every single night," she told fans in the audience. "This album probably also feels very happy and confident and free because that's the way that I get to feel every single day of my life because of my fiancé, who's here tonight."

Taylor added as a nod to her "The Fate of Ophelia" lyrics, "So, thanks for all the vibes."

Ahead of their highly anticipated wedding, the couple enjoyed a PDA-filled date night at a New York Knicks vs. Cleveland Cavaliers game in Travis' hometown.

With comets out of the picture, attention now turns to asteroids or even Earth itself as the source of prebiotic chemistry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet.

Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth.

Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement.

Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets.For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely.

Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves.

In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS.

The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second).Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke."

It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet.

However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth.

Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA.

However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars, because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity."This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet."

More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1, where all the planets are bunched up close.

In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive.

The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#814. Burnham urges caution on scrapping 3pm TV blackout

The blackout originated in the 1960s when Burnley chairman Bob Lord encouraged the EFL to oppose television coverage of 15:00 Saturday matches

Andy Burnham has urged caution on lifting the Saturday 3pm TV blackout in the UK, saying the health of the football pyramid should come first.

The rule was introduced in the 1960s to encourage fans to attend lower league games and prevents matches from being shown on UK television between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on Saturdays.

The blackout, which is enforced by Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes and is imposed by the English and Scottish football associations, comes into effect when 50% of fixtures in the top two divisions are scheduled to kick off at 3pm.

The Premier League is in the middle of a record Â£6.7bn domestic TV deal for Sky and TNT to show up to 270 live games a season.

But there could be room for change with the 3pm rule in the upcoming broadcast cycle, as the rights deals for the Premier League, EFL and SPFL all end in 2028-29.

The prime minister said any decision to remove the ban would require careful thought about the consequences.

"I would urge a bit of caution [on the blackout], because it does protect the income of lower-league clubs," Burnham said.

Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end

Why does football have Saturday 3pm TV blackout in UK?

"If you have effectively wall-to-wall Premier League football at any time, it takes away perhaps the incentive to go and watch the football league or non-league.

"So I think it has to be considered carefully. I'm not going to take the pure consumer view here. I'll take the health-of-football approach to this particular issue."

Only the FA Cup final, which traditionally kicks off at 3pm, is allowed to be broadcast during the blackout window.

In October, the SPFL said it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the TV new deal, which BBC Sport understands includes matches shown on a Saturday afternoon.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters has previously said a decision about whether the blackout stays in place would need to be made in the future.

But Burnham added: "I would first of all want to protect the football pyramid before I agree to saying 'let's have even more live football'".

"I think it's about protecting the experience with the paying supporter, protecting the football pyramid. Those issues matter to me, first of all."

#811. Belgium's Lukaku retires from internationals

Romelu Lukaku scored three goals for Belgium at the World Cup this summer

Romelu Lukaku has retired from international football, saying he has "enjoyed every single moment" of playing for Belgium.

Fenerbahce striker Lukaku, 33, made his international debut in 2010 and is Belgium's all-time leading men's goalscorer with 94 goals in 135 appearances.

He is the fifth highest men's international goalscorer of all time, behind Sunil Chhetri, Ali Daei, Lionel Messi and leader Cristiano Ronaldo, who has scored 146.

Lukaku scored eight goals across four World Cups, including in the run to the quarter-finals at this summer's tournament, and a total of six goals at three European Championships.

Writing on Instagram,, external the former Everton, Chelsea and Manchester United forward thanked his team-mates and coaches "for pushing and trusting me to help the team" during his 16 years with the national side.

He missed Belgium's Nations League win over Turkey last week with a hip injury and was an unused substitute on Sunday as they qualified for the last eight of the competition by beating Italy 4-1.

"These 16 years I gave all I had for the national team... I went through every emotion possible," Lukaku wrote.

"To the Belgium fans thank you for the support you gave our team. I am proud to have represented my country in four World Cups and three European Championships.

"I will never forget those moments. I'm at peace with my decision to stop here. It was amazing. It was enjoyable. I'm grateful."

In 2023, Lukaku scored 14 times in eight Euro 2024 qualifying appearances, breaking the record for goals scored by a player in a European Championship qualifying campaign.

His Belgium team-mate Kevin de Bruyne posted an image of himself with Lukaku, external on Instagram adding: "There are no words to describe what you've meant to me and our country!"

#810. French football head Philippe Diallo is shock contender to fight Infantino for Fifa job

Diallo may have candidacy confirmed by Uefa on Tuesday

Uefa executive committee meeting to discuss matter

The French Football Federation president, Philippe Diallo, is a surprise late contender to run for the Fifa presidency and could have his candidacy confirmed by Tuesday. The search for a Uefa-backed candidate to run against Gianni Infantino has been taken to the wire, with Wednesday the deadline for those planning to contest the Fifa election in March.

Diallo has emerged as the favourite after plans to enlist a decorated former player or manager did not reach fruition, although other names are understood to remain under consideration. Uefa’s executive committee will discuss the matter on Monday and the approval of its 55 member associations would be sought.

Diallo strongly criticised Infantino in September, saying he had “seriously damaged the image and unity of football”. He continued: “His initiatives during and after the World Cup have seriously damaged the image and the unity of football. As a result, we believe that trust has been broken.”

It is unclear whether a move to back Diallo would spell the end of the campaign begun by Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japanese Football Association, to challenge Infantino. Tashima, a Fifa council member, has influential backers within Uefa but its hierarchy may conclude Diallo has a greater chance of wooing voters in other areas of the world.

Diallo would be expected to win the backing of the vast majority of Uefa’s member associations and there are hopes he could pick up votes from Francophone members of the Confederation of African Football, which has been steadfast in its support for Infantino.

There are concerns that having multiple challengers to Infantino will strengthen his position and play into the hands of a campaign that will present the incumbent as the unity candidate after months of in-fighting.

Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, has been reluctant to endorse an alternative candidate, despite opposing Infantino, with some federations arguing that a boycott of the election would send the strongest message regarding the need for governance reform.

Should a career administrator such as Diallo be granted Uefa’s backing it would be a marked departure from its original approach, in which it sought to coalesce behind a more high-profile figure who had made their name on the pitch or in the dugout. There had been late hope that Arsène Wenger, Fifa’s chief of global development, would throw put himself forward, but it would have required a major change of heart from him. Former players such as Mikaël Silvestre and, belatedly, Didier Drogba are understood to have expressed interest that never came to anything

Germany’s head coach, Jürgen Klopp, has said he would welcome a new president. “The general consensus is that a change might make sense. But what would interest me even more in this context, from a football perspective, is that we never thought things could get any worse after Sepp Blatter, and yet someone actually managed to make it worse.

“Right now, we’re thinking that if Mr Infantino were to leave, it would be cool if the next person could just do a better job. Because I believe it should be possible to do better.”

How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead.

This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo.

Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable?

In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock.

For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it.

Using a technique called spectroscopy, astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star.

However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance.

Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere.

A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise.

A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere.

Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star.

The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences.

For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet.

Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air?

In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe.

Atmospheric pressure matters just as much. At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs.

Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal.

But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there?

Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth. This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far.

Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed.

The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation.

Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star.

Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge.

The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster.

We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets.

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Alix is an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham specialising in the characterisation of stars and exoplanets. She is passionate about science communication, and how astrophysics is portrayed in movies, TV, and pop culture at large.

#807. Cap fits as Robertson poised to take King Kenny's crown

You've done Liverpool and Scotland proud - Kenny Dalglish on Andy Robertson's career

Andy Robertson will become the most capped men's Scotland international if he earns his 103rd cap in Monday night's Nations League campaign closer in Switzerland.

Twelve years on from his debut - off the bench in a Poland friendly - he is set to surpass his friend and fellow Liverpool legend, Kenny Dalglish, whose record haul has stood for 40 years.

On moving level with the man they - and he - will always call King, the Tottenham Hotspur left-back shifted chat towards the former forward, his commendable humility laid bare.

But, in St Gallen, the spotlight will be brightly shone on one of Scotland's favourite sons as he goes solo at the summit.

Robertson set to make history, but hero Dalglish will always be King

Inside the fairytale journey of Scotland captain Robertson

Andy Robertson on his hero, Kenny Dalglish

For much of this year, Dalglish was the only man to have pulled on the navy blue of Scotland more times than Robertson.

'King Kenny' topped the list on 102 caps - earning his last in November 1986 against Luxembourg when in a player-manager role at Liverpool.

Few since have even come close to toppling him - even when Robertson does, he is keen to stress the throne is still reserved for Dalglish - but it is perhaps fitting it is the current captain, given their great friendship.

Which allows Dalglish to say he's not having any of it.

"He always says: 'You've got millions more games. Nations League, what's that? They didn't have that in my day!'" Robertson joked on the Stick to Football podcast recently.

"I think he might bring up a ratio for years-to-games-played so he's still on top.

"It's obviously something that's been on my radar for a while now. When you get to 80-odd caps, you start to look up."

Dalglish can console himself that his record of 30 goals - held jointly with Denis Law - is safely out of Robertson's reach.

But not out of John McGinn's - the midfielder's double against North Macedonia on Friday having taken him to within six of the legendary duo.

The Aston Villa captain is lurking only eight caps behind Robertson on the all-time caps list, too, so the Scotland men's centurion club could have three members soon.

Since being given the armband by Alex McLeish after Scott Brown retired in 2018, Robertson has captained Scotland 32 times more than any other player.

At the time, he had earned just 22 caps and was just 24 but had established himself as Liverpool's left-back as they reached the Champions League final.

Now he is the only man to have led Scotland out at three major finals, reaching the milestone at the World Cup this summer.

Scotland and Napoli midfielder Scott McTominay enthused: "He's such a great captain and he's got that good balance between being one of the senior players and saying you need to wake up if you're not playing well.

"Then he's also got the personable side, organising things with the manager, helping young players and stuff. He's brilliant with that, brilliant."

One of those young players is 20-year-old Findlay Curtis, who told the media the night before Robertson's potentially-historic night that his captain has "probably been the biggest role model" he's looked up to since joining the international set-up earlier this year.

Perhaps that was because Robertson did him a turn back in the day. Unbeknownst to the skipper.

Rangers winger Curtis was only 14 during the Covid pandemic and was partial to playing a bit of Fifa, and Robertson was a star in his team.

"I was just thinking, I had him in my Fifa team," he explained. "[For] defending and he was just fast as well.

"What a servant he has been for the country."

'I had him in my Fifa team!' - Findlay Curtis on going from fan to team-mate of Robertson

Robertson has played under four permanent Scotland team bosses in his 12-year international career.

It was Strachan who plucked him from the under-21s to hand him his debut as a 19-year-old in a win over Poland in March 2014.

McLeish made him captain in 2018, calling Robertson the "outstanding candidate" and an "inspirational figure" - and now he has played five times for new boss Sebastien Pocognoli.

He even played one game under interim manager Malky Mackay in a friendly against the Netherlands at Pittodrie in 2017 as the Scottish FA searched for Strachan's replacement.

However, it is Steve Clarke's seven-year stint that Robertson will be mainly associated with, as the pair led Scotland to three major tournaments.

Robertson played 68 times for Clarke, all of them as captain, and the recently departed head coach consistently praised his figurehead.

"He's been a fantastic captain for Scotland," Clarke said at the World Cup.

"He's worked ever so hard for the country and he leads the group like the leader he is - and he's very, very important to me and the squad."

Over the piece, Robertson's caps are spread fairly evenly among friendlies and qualification games.

Crucially, though, he has also played nine times in major tournaments. What will rankle with him is there is only one win among those nine - June's victory over Haiti in Boston at the World Cup.

Overall, though, Robertson's Scotland career can be characterised by consistency.

He has started 100 of his 102 caps, rarely ever being substituted. He has not missed a camp in three years.

The only question seems to be how many Scotland caps will Robertson end up with?

At 32 and still playing in the Premier League, it appears there will be plenty more to come.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program and set the stage for the Apollo progam to land on the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin. NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks.

Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program. Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11, and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13.

Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon.

It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11.

"This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview. "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station. As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water."

The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle.

During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon.

Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral.

As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#805. Klopp says Infantino worse than Blatter

Jurgen Klopp took over as Germany head coach in July

Germany manager Jurgen Klopp says he "didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that" as he called for Fifa president Gianni Infantino to be replaced.

Blatter resigned as Fifa boss in 2015 amid a corruption scandal and was succeeded by Infantino in February 2016.

Infantino plans to stand for re-election in March but has been under pressure since scrapping his Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, which included selling off stakes in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

Infantino apologised to the Fifa Council for the plan but was told he was not fit to lead world football's governing body unless he released all the documents and answered key questions.

"I've been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense," said Klopp.

"I didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that."

Klopp added: "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job."

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Infantino apologises to Fifa Council - but told he is still not fit to lead

Uefa - European football's governing body - has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down.

It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released.

The deadline for candidates to officially confirm they are standing against Infantino in Fifa's presidential election is Wednesday.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, who is Fifa's head of global development, had been considering running for the job but sources have told BBC Sport he has ruled himself out.

Uefa is said to still be hopeful of finding an alternative candidate before Wednesday's deadline.

Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega was the first person to put his name forward in October.

Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima has also announced his intention to stand.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football - people who aren't driven by financial interests," said Klopp.

"If someone like that were to step up - if someone like that were to become president - I think that would be a significant improvement.

"There are surely people who care deeply about the future of football and have no financial interests in it."

#804. Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon

Far below the ocean's surface, a constant snowfall drifts through the darkness. But unlike the frozen flakes that fall from the sky, this underwater snow consists of tiny clumps of waste, dead organisms, and other debris. Known as marine snow, these particles contain everything from mucus and animal feces to silt and the remains of microscopic plankton.

As this material sinks, it carries enormous quantities of carbon from the upper ocean toward the seafloor. Researchers estimate that marine snow removes more than 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters each year. Yet only about two gigatons reach depths where that carbon can remain stored for hundreds or even thousands of years.

Why so much carbon fails to make it into the deep ocean has long puzzled scientists. Now, researchers from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have identified a surprisingly important factor: how sticky the marine snow is.

Their findings, published October 8 in the journal Science, show that the viscosity, or thickness and gooeyness, of marine snow influences how quickly bacteria break it apart and how far it can sink. According to the researchers, the stickiest particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as particles with a thinner, less viscous consistency.

Marine snow plays an important role in Earth's carbon cycle, the natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms. By transporting carbon into deep water, sinking particles can keep some of it isolated from the atmosphere for centuries or longer.

However, not every particle survives the journey. Bacteria feed on marine snow as it descends, gradually breaking down the material and affecting how much carbon reaches the ocean's depths.

The new research provides the first detailed look at how living bacteria interact with the physical structure of marine snow and, more broadly, mucus itself. These interactions are important well beyond the ocean's carbon cycle. Similar relationships between bacteria and mucus help sustain coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive systems of humans and other animals.

Until recently, scientists lacked the technology to observe these interactions at the microscopic scale needed to understand them.

A Four-Year Quest to See Inside Marine Snow

The project began in 2021, when Bryce Inman, then a postdoctoral researcher at Scripps Oceanography, set out to explore what he calls "the muscoscape."

"Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible," said Inman.

Together with colleagues including Farooq Azam, a microbiologist and professor emeritus at Scripps, Inman spent four years trying to overcome that limitation. Multiple attempts were unsuccessful before the team finally developed a working technique in 2025.

Their solution combined 3D confocal microscopy with specially designed fluorescent molecules. Confocal microscopy uses light to capture detailed images at different depths within a sample, allowing researchers to reconstruct its structure in three dimensions. The fluorescent molecules helped make features of the material visible.

For the first time, the scientists could examine the "physical terrain" of individual marine snow particles while watching how living bacteria moved through and interacted with them.

The images revealed a surprisingly intricate microscopic environment, complete with structural differences that affect where bacteria can settle and how easily they can reach the material inside.

Much like snowflakes in the atmosphere, marine snow particles vary considerably. Each contains its own mixture of organic and inorganic materials, creating differences in composition, structure, and viscosity.

The researchers' new imaging approach, described in a companion study published in Nature Communications, revealed that bacteria preferentially colonize areas near a particle's surface where the material is less viscous.

The denser, stickier regions deeper inside are much harder for bacteria to penetrate.

"Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down," said Inman. "Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through"

This difference has important consequences for how long marine snow remains intact.

In laboratory experiments, the scientists observed that particles with greater viscosity resisted bacterial degradation and fragmentation for longer periods. Computer simulations further suggested that these stickier particles can descend to greater depths before breaking apart.

Based on these results, the team estimates that highly viscous marine snow can deliver more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.

The findings help explain why some sinking material transports carbon much farther into the ocean than other particles, even though both begin their journeys near the surface.

"How far marine snow can sink is a surprisingly complicated problem, and we have added another - very gooey - piece to the puzzle," said Inman.

A Discovery With Implications Beyond the Ocean

Although the research focuses on marine snow, its implications extend to many environments where bacteria interact with mucus.

Mucus is often regarded as a relatively simple, slippery substance. But the new imaging technology reveals that it has a complex internal landscape, with microscopic structures that can influence how bacteria behave.

Understanding these physical features could help scientists investigate biological processes in settings ranging from human digestive health to the recovery of damaged coral reefs.

The method also opens opportunities to explore interactions that previously could not be observed directly, providing researchers with a new way to study the microscopic environments inhabited by bacteria.

Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, "has a surprising amount of structure," Inman said. "There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we're really examining this physical habitat."

The discovery adds an important missing piece to scientists' understanding of how carbon travels through the ocean. It also demonstrates that something as seemingly ordinary as the thickness of underwater slime can have far-reaching consequences for the planet's natural systems.

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Simons Foundation and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.

#803. Nara Smith Reveals She’s Never Decorated for Christmas

Nara Smith exclusively revealed to E! News that before this year, she’s never decorated her house for the holidays.

Nara Smith wasn’t traditionally one to haul out the holly.

The influencer—who shares kids Rumble Honey, 6, Slim Easy, 4, Whimsy Lou, 2, and Fawnie Golden, 13 months, with husband Lucky Blue Smith—revealed that before this year, getting into the Christmas spirit didn’t involve any decking of the halls at her house.

“I think I'm going to decorate for Christmas,” she told E! News’ Erin Lim Rhodes of the upcoming holiday season while at the 2026 Baby2Baby Gala hosted by Paul Mitchell Nov. 14, “which I've never really done before.”

But festive decorations aren’t the only memories the TikToker plans on whipping up from scratch.

She added that her family’s Christmas will also include “a lot of German traditions,” noting, “I'm from Germany, so incorporating all of that and having the kids grow up with that is really important for me.”

Plus, the kitchen connoisseur—whose calming videos detailing her efforts to make foods from scratch at home earned her a massive social media following—naturally has some ideas about how to sweeten the most wonderful time of the year.

In the meantime, she and Lucky—who is also dad to 9-year-old Gravity Blue with ex Stormi Bree—are enjoying getting the opportunity to get into the giving spirit of Christmas a little early with Baby2Baby, whose mission is to provide the basic necessities to babies in need.

For Nara, the motivation for getting involved with Baby2Baby is as simple as “us having four kids,” adding she appreciates how the nonprofit is “always advocating” for children and parents that need that vital assistance.

As she noted, “There being any need for fundamental items as a parent—I can't even imagine how stressful it is. And the fact that Baby2Baby is really advocating for that is really important.”

As for her own life at home as a young mom of four, Nara has been clear she’s always envisioned motherhood at an early age.

“I wanted kids younger. I didn’t know how young, but I knew I didn’t want to be an old mom,” she said on the Oct. 8 episode of the Aspire podcast. “My dad, he had us at 45. He said, ‘I wish I would have had you earlier because [of] my energy.' He had a transparent conversation with us about it, and I saw that and heard him.”

And though four babies wasn’t always in the exact plan, Nara and Lucky wouldn’t have it any other way.

"I have two siblings, so I was like, 'You know what, I really like the number of three—so let's have three,'" she explained. "And then our fourth baby was a surprise. She was not supposed to be here, but now she's the most precious thing and I couldn't imagine my life without her."

The Oscar winner, who has worked with organizations like UNICEF and is a UN Goodwill Ambassador, makes it a priority to share those same humanitarian values with her six children.

"With my family, I'm trying to raise them to have respect for all people and make friends around the world and feel at home with the world and really live a truly global [life]," she told NBC News in 2011. "I think it's what forms them and it's really important to me."

"I know it’s cliché, but I love everything, even the hard parts," the Kardashians star—mom to daughter True and son Tatum with ex Tristan Thompson—said of motherhood in a 2022 interview with Elle. "[My kids] challenge me as a person, and being able to shape little people into really incredible big people is an honor and a gift."

"We have to take those roles seriously, especially in today’s day and age, with how much accessibility children have and the information they’re exposed to so young," she added. "It’s super scary, but I take my job very seriously. I love it so much."

"I have such unconditional love for my kids," the Keep Up With the Kardashians alum—who shares North, Saint, Chicago and Psalm with ex-husband Kanye West—wrote on her website in 2017. "No matter what, I will always love them and support them in anything they choose to do in life."

"My family was so close growing up; now that I'm a mom, I understand the bond my mom and dad felt with us," she continued. "There can be ups and downs with kids but no matter what, I always learn so much from them. Being a mom is the most important job I have."

In a 2018 interview, the Kylie Cosmetics founder shared how much her mindset has changed since giving birth to Stormi that year.

"I think more about the future because of her. Every time I leave and I'm stressed about leaving her, I'm like, ‘I'm doing it for you,'" Kylie—who also shares son Aire with ex Travis Scott—told London Evening Standard. "Everyone says you change completely when you become a mom, but I really feel the same, just better."

The Poosh creator shares kids Mason, Penelope and Reign with ex Scott Disick. She's also mom to son Rocky with husband Travis Barker.

"It's definitely my favorite role in life," she said of motherhood in a 2012 interview with Parents. "It has changed me and made me realize there is nothing else I would rather do with my time. Being a mom is what life is about. I hope people realize what the priorities in life should be and know not everything has to be perfect."

As mom to kids Camden, Jaxon and Saylor with ex Jay Cutler, the Laguna Beach alum told Modeliste Magazine in 2016, "There's just so much more love in your life. I finally feel like I have a real identity"

"I feel like I have a purpose here in life now," she added. "I'm a mom to these three amazing little babies, and my whole world just kind of opened up."

"As soon as I found out I was pregnant," the Pretty Little Liars actress—who shares daughters Atlas and Rome with Matte Babel—said in a 2023 interview with Byrdie, "I put the old version of myself aside, and a new chapter began."

"I never want my children to say I work too much," she continued. "When I'm putting them to bed or having a meal with them, I put my phone down. They're growing up so quickly, and I don't want to look back and think, 'I missed this because of a work function.'"

The Lizzie McGuire alum is mom to son Luca with her ex-husband Mike Comrie. she also shares daughters Banks, Mae and Townes with husband Matthew Koma.

"I don't always balance it all," she admitted of her parenting duties in a 2018 interview with E! News, "I do the best that I can, and some months are crazier than others."

Still, Duff considers herself "a mother first."

"My decision-making process is like, 'Hey can I make this work?'" she said of finding family time in her busy work life. "I've been doing this for a while so I do have a strong work ethic, and I have a lot of people around me that help keep my schedule straight and plan and know where my priorities lie."

The powerhouse singer is a huge inspiration to all of us, but turns out the mother of Blue, Rumi and Sir—who she shares with husband Jay-Z—also makes sure to be the same for her own children.

"It just gives you purpose and all of the things that my self-esteem was associated it, it's all completely different," she said of motherhood in a 2012 interview with Anderson Cooper. "I realized why I was born and more than anything all of the things I want to pass onto my child and the best way of doing that is not by preaching or telling her but showing her by example."

For the Devil Wears Prada star, becoming a mom was a groundbreaking experience in both personal and work life.

“I don't think it's necessary to be a mother to play a mother. I think that should be open to lots of different actors," she told People in 2024, adding that welcoming sons Jonathan and Jack with husband Adam Shulman helped her gain an understanding of "the depth of love" maternal characters can feel.

The Mindy Project actress—who is mom to kids Katherine, Spencer and Anne—said she feels "so much more happy and confident after having children."

"In each subsequent year of my life, I'm just feeling happier and happier," she told ABC News in 2021, "and I am amazed at that,"

Though she played one of the titular Bad Moms in the 2016 comedy, the actress couldn't be a better parent to her kids Wyatt and Dimitri, who she shares with Ashton Kurcher.

"I reprioritized my life, in all honesty," Kunis said of her motherhood journey in a 2016 interview with Entertainment Tonight. "I traveled through all my 20s and I was very selfish—in a good way, not in a way I regret. And I think having a kid made me realize how incredibly selfless I want to be."

The Transformers actress—who shares kids Noah, Bodhi and Journey with her ex-husband Brian Austin Green, as well as daugther Saga with ex-fiancé Machine Gun Kelly—has a lovely approach to her parenting style.

"I don't think I need to teach my children with harsh words or with punishment. I believe that if I love them the right way, there's no need for that," she told Harper's Bazaar Arabia in 2015. "I'm a free-spirit mother."

The Gossip Girl alum and Ryan Reynolds' couple goals include being amazing parents to four children, including all the funny moments that come with being a parent.

"It's tough when you get pooped on and barfed on, but having a baby is wonderful," Lively joked to NW Magazine in 2016. "Even when it's tough and I'm exhausted, I think, 'I am so fortunate.'"
